outline.chapter_title: Introduction to Text‑to‑Image Diffusion and the Need for Controlled Fine‑tuning
outline.description: Sets the stage by reviewing modern text‑to‑image diffusion models, their capabilities, and why downstream control (subject‑driven and controllable generation) is challenging. Introduces the desiderata for fine‑tuning methods.
subtopics: Overview of large‑scale text‑to‑image diffusion (Stable Diffusion, DALL‑E 2, Imagen, etc.)
Limitations of plain textual prompting
Two downstream tasks: subject‑driven generation and controllable generation
Desiderata for fine‑tuning: training efficiency and preservation of generative quality
Shortcomings of existing fine‑tuning approaches (small‑LR updates, LoRA, adapters)

outline.chapter_title: Geometric Perspective on Neural Representations: Hyperspherical Energy
outline.description: Introduces hyperspherical energy as a tool to measure pairwise angular relationships among neurons, explains why angular information encodes semantics, and motivates its use as a preservation metric.
subtopics: Definition of hyperspherical energy and relation to cosine similarity
Why angles matter: sphere‑net results and toy auto‑encoder experiment
Interpretation of hyperspherical energy as a measure of semantic structure
Limitations of Euclidean distance as a fine‑tuning metric

outline.chapter_title: Orthogonal Transformations and Their Invariance Properties
outline.description: Explains the mathematical property that orthogonal matrices preserve pairwise angles, providing the theoretical foundation for Orthogonal Fine‑tuning (OFT).
subtopics: Orthogonal matrices: definition, rotation vs. reflection, special orthogonal group
Proof that hyperspherical energy is invariant under a common orthogonal transformation
Intuition from Fourier phase vs. magnitude analogy
Why preserving angles is a sweet spot between flexibility and regularity

outline.description: Derives the OFT objective, shows how it replaces conventional gradient updates with a learned orthogonal matrix per layer, and details the training pipeline.
subtopics: Formal statement of the OFT optimization problem
Layer‑wise orthogonal transformation: W = R·W⁰
Initialization (R = I) and gradient‑based learning of R
Comparison with standard fine‑tuning and LoRA in terms of objectives

outline.description: Presents practical ways to represent and learn orthogonal matrices at scale, including Cayley transform and block‑diagonal structures.
subtopics: Cayley transform: R = (I+Q)(I–Q)⁻¹ with Q skew‑symmetric
(Limited) expressivity to SO(d) and its practical impact
Block‑diagonal orthogonal matrices: reducing O(d²) to O(d²/r)
Optional block sharing to achieve O(d²/r²)
Parameter count comparison with LoRA; concrete numeric example

outline.description: Extends OFT by adding an explicit radius constraint that keeps R close to the identity matrix, improving stability.
subtopics: Motivation for an ε‑ball around I
"R – I" norm constraint formulation
Incorporating the constraint via projected gradient on Q after Cayley transform
Effect of ε on flexibility vs. preservation (illustrative plots)
Relationship between COFT, OFT, and traditional small‑learning‑rate fine‑tuning

outline.\ndescription: "Re‑scaled OFT" augments OFT with a diagonal scaling matrix D so that both direction and magnitude can be adapted without affecting hyperspherical energy.
\nsubtopics: "Why magnitude matters after direction is fixed"
"Learning D jointly with R; negligible extra cost"
